Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

fastsae 1.0.0

Estimation engines for hb_area(), hb_unit() and hb_twofold()

  • New argument engine, taking an engine object from the new constructors inla_engine() and jax_engine() (or the strings "inla", the default, and "jax" for their default settings). Each constructor holds all settings of its engine, so hb_area() itself only describes the model:
    • inla_engine(strategy, link, scale_model, prior_prec, prior_phi, prior_rho, prior_prec_time, prior_rho_time, prior_prec_subarea, draws, seed, ...), where ... goes to INLA::inla(). control.* lists given there are merged with the package defaults (before, they clashed with them in hb_area() and replaced them in hb_unit()/hb_twofold()). Priors and draws left at NULL take the default of the model function, so the defaults of each function are unchanged; settings a function does not use are ignored with a warning.
    • jax_engine(warmup, samples, chains, device, seed, prior_beta, robust, keep_draws, progress) fits the same area-level models by full MCMC (NumPyro NUTS on JAX: CPU, NVIDIA GPU or the Apple silicon GPU via device = "metal") through ‘reticulate’ (Suggests); the engine formerly shipped in the separate ‘fastsaegpu’ package now lives in fastsae. It supports all six families, bym2/bym/besag/generic1 (alias "leroux"), rw1/ar1/iid and every st_interaction, plus prior_beta = "horseshoe" and robust = TRUE (Student-t area effects). Results have the same structure as the INLA engine, with the posterior draws in draws, the largest split R-hat in rhat_max (convergence is rhat_max < 1.05), and DIC/WAIC in goodness. Posterior self-benchmarking (also by benchmark_group) adjusts the MCMC draws exactly as for INLA, and benchmark_sae() uses the draws for the MSE matrix.
    • The engine settings are returned in engine_spec; engine holds the engine name.
  • hb_twofold() also takes engine = jax_engine() (or "jax"): the two-fold model with an iid, Besag or BYM2 area effect and an iid sub-area effect is sampled by NumPyro NUTS, for the Gaussian, binomial and Poisson families, and the area aggregates in df_area come from the MCMC draws. Against INLA on simulated data (20 areas) the area means correlated above 0.999 and differed by a median of 0.02-0.07 posterior SD (the priors differ: half-normal standard deviations instead of PC priors); a fit took 7-11 s against 11-31 s for INLA with the area aggregates. The result has the structure of the INLA engine plus draws, rhat_max, device and elapsed_seconds.
  • hb_unit() also takes engine = jax_engine() (or "jax"): the nested error model (Gaussian, Bernoulli or Poisson units; iid, Besag or BYM2 domain effects) is sampled by NumPyro NUTS from the sampled units, and the domain means, including the finite population mean with popsize_var, are summarised from the MCMC draws. Checked against a Stan fit of the same model and priors (30 domains; domain means within 0.04 posterior SD, SDs within 5%), and, with their own priors, against hbsae::fSAE(method = "HB") (Gaussian; within 0.1 SD) and the INLA engine (within 0.06 SD). On cornsoybean (12 counties) the priors matter: the county SDs are 1.1-1.4 times INLA’s and 0.8-1.0 times hbsae’s.
  • The NumPyro backend returns the draws of the residual variance (sigma2_e) and can return the draws of selected rows only (draw_rows).
  • Convergence diagnostics for jax_engine() fits (Vehtari et al., 2021), identical to posterior::rhat(), ess_bulk() and ess_tail() (checked to 1e-10): the rank-normalized split R-hat and bulk/tail ESS of every hyperparameter, coefficient and area parameter in mcmc_diagnostics, with ess_min, divergences (divergent transitions) and treedepth_hits. rhat_max used to cover only the coefficients and the area parameters, with the classic split R-hat, so a variance whose chains had not mixed went unnoticed: on mys without vardir (2 x 300 draws) the residual variance had R-hat 1.13 and a bulk ESS of 14, with 13 divergent transitions. Fits warn for R-hat >= 1.05, ESS below 100 per chain and divergent transitions (class fastsae_mcmc_warning), inform for R-hat between 1.01 and 1.05, and print() shows the ESS and divergences.
  • autoplot(fit, type = "trace") and type = "rank" plot the chains of a jax_engine() fit: the hyperparameters, coefficients and the area with the largest R-hat by default, or any pars, with R-hat and ESS in the panel labels.
  • jax_engine(): the WAIC of a Gaussian model with an unknown residual variance (hb_area() without vardir, hb_unit()) used the posterior mean of the residual SD in every draw; it now uses the SD of each draw (on mys: 129.3 instead of 135.9).
  • jax_engine(): the temporal = "ar1" effect sums to zero over the periods (as "rw1" already did) when the model has an intercept, which then carries the mean level. Over a few periods the level of a stationary AR(1) effect traded off against the intercept along a ridge whose width depends on rho, and NUTS reported divergent transitions: on sim_panel (5 years, 4 x 1000 draws, 4 seeds) 30-201 before and 1-6 after, with the area estimates 0.11 instead of 0.21 posterior SD from INLA; with st_interaction = "type2", 14-57 before and 0 after. With spatial = "bym2" one of 4 seeds still gave 38 (3-4 for the others; 30-154 before), which a longer warmup reduces. The INLA engine keeps its unconstrained AR(1) effect, so the intercepts of the two engines differ by the mean of the time effects (the area estimates are not affected by this).
  • hb_unit() checks that the unit responses are 0 or 1 for family = "binomial" and non-negative integers for "poisson".
  • print() failed on a fit whose call holds braces, e.g. from do.call() with a function object: the call was read as cli markup.
  • jax_engine(robust = TRUE) is documented as what it does: Student-t random effects (it was described as Student-t sampling errors for the Gaussian family).
  • hb_unit() and hb_twofold() take the same engine = inla_engine(...). In hb_twofold(), prior_prec_area is now inla_engine(prior_prec = ), n_samples is inla_engine(draws = ), and the posterior draws for the area aggregates honour seed. Their results carry engine and engine_spec too.
  • jax_engine(device = "metal") now samples on the Apple GPU. jax-metal cannot compile two operations of NumPyro’s NUTS sampler (the popcnt bit count, and lax.cond statements whose outputs are constants), so fits used to fall back to the CPU. fastsae now replaces both with equivalent operations that Metal can compile, and steps the chains from Python; the draws match the CPU sampler. On an Apple M4, Metal is faster than the CPU for large models (about 2x at 10,000 domains) and slower for small ones, where a fixed cost of about two minutes per fit dominates (see the “hb_area() engines” benchmark article). device = "auto" keeps using the CPU on macOS.
  • New setup_numpyro_env() to install the Python side, and setup_numpyro_env(check_only = TRUE) to check it. Nothing is installed or downloaded by the check. It looks only at an initialised Python, RETICULATE_PYTHON / RETICULATE_PYTHON_ENV and the r-numpyro-gpu environment, so it answers in about a second instead of searching the whole system for Python installations (which took over 20 s on Windows).
  • The frequentist lme4 GLMM route (method = "laplace" for non-spatial binomial and Poisson models) has been removed; such models are now fitted by INLA. ‘lme4’ moved to Suggests.
  • Deprecated: method (method = "laplace" becomes engine = inla_engine(strategy = "laplace")), and passing strategy, link, scale_model, prior_*, benchmark_draws, benchmark_seed, n_samples or INLA::inla() arguments directly to hb_area(), hb_unit() or hb_twofold(). They still work, with a warning, and are forwarded to inla_engine().
  • print()/summary() show the engine, and the self-benchmarking line now names the method used (posterior draws or Wang-Fuller-Qu) instead of always reporting Wang-Fuller-Qu.

Covariate selection: step_sae()

  • New step_sae() selects the covariates of any fitted model by stepwise search (backward, forward or both), refitting it with the same settings (family, spatial or temporal structure, engine) at every step.
    • EBLUP models: AIC, BIC (default) or KIC from the full log-likelihood (Marhuenda, Morales and Pardo 2014). Models with a method argument are fitted by ML during the search and the selected model is refitted with the original method. On mys with a noise covariate the path and the BIC values equal those of emdi::step().
    • HB models of every family: LCPO (leave-one-out through INLA’s conditional predictive ordinates; default with inla_engine()), WAIC (default with jax_engine()) or DIC. WAIC is unstable with one observation per area: in a binomial simulation it selected exactly the true covariates in 27% of the replicates, LCPO in 70% (benchmarks/validation/step_sae.R).
    • Spatial models are selected with their spatial effect: a spatially smooth noise covariate was kept in 20% of the replicates by the Fay-Herriot model and in 8% by the spatial one (spatial confounding; Hodges and Reich 2010).
  • eblup_bhf() returns goodness (full log-likelihood, AIC and BIC), as the other EBLUP models; with method = "ML" they equal those of lme4::lmer(REML = FALSE).

Agreement metrics in compare_sae()

  • compare_sae() no longer reports Pearson’s correlation: two reasonable models of the same data correlate almost perfectly whatever their differences, and a correlation measures association, not agreement. It now reports the mean difference and 95% limits of agreement (Bland and Altman 1986), Lin’s (1989) concordance correlation coefficient, the differences relative to the RMSE of the first model, the mean change of rank and the overlap of the highest and lowest domains (new argument top, default 10%), besides Spearman’s correlation and the MSE and RSE comparisons. The numbers are also returned as $agreement, and the domain table gains ranks and z_diff. autoplot(type = "difference") is a Bland-Altman plot.

Default priors of the HB models

  • The random-effect standard deviations of Gaussian HB models (hb_area(), hb_unit(), hb_twofold(); area, sub-area, time and interaction effects) get a half-normal prior with the scale of the response, sd(y), by default. It replaces INLA’s PC prior P(σ>1)=0.01P(\sigma > 1) = 0.01 (hb_area(), hb_twofold()) and the log-gamma(0.01, 0.01) prior (hb_unit()). The PC prior depends on the unit of the response: on mys with the response in tenths it moved the estimates by up to 4.1 posterior SD. In a simulation (benchmarks/validation/default_sd_prior.R) the 95% intervals covered 93-97% with the half-normal prior (EBLUP: 93-96%) and 85-95% with PC priors scaled to sd(y). The other families get a half-normal(1) prior on the link scale instead of the PC prior: for binomial and beta responses the intervals covered 93-95% against 92-94%, and the PC prior underestimated the area SD by up to 18% (benchmarks/validation/default_sd_prior_glm.R). With small samples (binomial and beta, 5-20 units per area) the PC prior covered 86-94% and estimated an area SD of 0.8 as 0.45; Poisson and binomial BYM2 models behaved as binomial and beta (benchmarks/validation/default_sd_prior_glm_more.R).
  • hb_area(family = "gamma") without vardir warns, with both engines, that the gamma precision is weakly identified: it is then estimated from one observation per area and trades off against the area effect, so it follows its prior. The prior is half-normal(10) on the precision with both engines (INLA used its default loggamma(1, 0.01)). In a simulation (benchmarks/validation/gamma_shape_prior.R) the estimate stayed at 8-13 for true shapes 5-100 and the 95% intervals covered 92-100%; INLA’s prior put it at 76-84 and covered 52-86% for shapes 5 and 20. Intervals are too wide when the sampling noise is small, and areas without a direct estimate covered 85-97%. With vardir the intervals covered 92-94% (benchmarks/validation/dispersion_vardir.R). Leroux’s λ\lambda gets a uniform prior. inla_engine(prior_prec = ) overrides the default as before.
  • jax_engine(priors = "inla"), the new default, gives the NumPyro engine the priors of inla_engine(): the default above, INLA’s PC prior on the BYM2 ϕ\phi (on INLA’s support of logit ϕ\phi), INLA’s prior on the AR(1) correlation and N(0,1000)N(0, 1000) coefficients. On mys the two engines now agree within 0.03 (iid) and 0.05 (BYM2) posterior SD, 0.35 before; the SAR example of test_hb_area_sar.R within 0.05 SD, 0.22 before. priors = "weakly_informative" keeps the previous priors.
  • hb_area(family = "gaussian") without vardir was unusable with inla_engine(): INLA’s default log-gamma(1, 5e-5) prior on the residual precision put the residual SD near zero, so the area means collapsed onto the direct estimates and the 95% intervals covered 0-4% of the true means (benchmarks/validation/likelihood_priors.R). The residual SD now gets the half-normal(sd y) prior of jax_engine() (94-97% coverage in every unit of y), as do the unit errors of hb_unit().
  • The beta precision without vardir or trials gets INLA’s log-gamma(1, 0.1) prior with both engines (jax_engine() used half-normal(10), which covered 84-97% against 88-96%).
  • hb_area(family = "beta", vardir = ) fixes the precision of each area at the posterior mean of a first fit, ϕd=μ̂d(1−μ̂d)/Vd−1\phi_d = \hat\mu_d(1 - \hat\mu_d)/V_d - 1, instead of at the direct estimate (two stages, with both engines, as the negative binomial size). With the direct estimate the model variance was Vdμd(1−μd)/(yd(1−yd))V_d \mu_d(1 - \mu_d)/(y_d(1 - y_d)), not VdV_d, and the 95% intervals covered 81-84% of the true proportions near 0.08, against 90-94% now (benchmarks/validation/beta_vardir_phi.R). tipsae’s precision at the model mean inside the model (type_disp = "var") covered 93-95% but its likelihood is bimodal: 11 of 240 fits did not converge.
  • The precision column of df_hb for such a model is the precision the model was fitted with; it still showed the precision at the direct estimate.
  • hb_area(family = "beta") warns that trials is ignored when vardir is also given.
  • jax_engine() computed the WAIC of a beta model with trials with a precision of 10 instead of nd−1n_d - 1.
  • New vignette “Default Priors of the Hierarchical Bayes Models”: the default priors of both engines and the simulations behind the choices. It also writes out the three models with all their default priors (including the Leroux, SAR and SLM correlations, the space-time interactions and the coefficients under benchmark_method = "wfq"), shows how to list the priors of a fit with INLA::inla.priors.used() and when to change them.
  • The documentation no longer describes the earlier priors as the defaults: ?hb_twofold (which still contrasted the half-normal priors of jax_engine() with PC priors of inla_engine()), the unit-level vignette (re-run on cornsoybean: the two engines now agree within Monte Carlo error and INLA matches the exact posterior within 0.06 posterior SD), the INLA vignette (which also gave a wrong formula for INLA’s approximation and the plug-in beta precision) and the finite population vignette, whose simulations were re-run with the default priors (coverage of the 95% intervals 92-93%, against 88-89% with the PC prior and the plug-in beta precision used before).

Gamma and negative binomial dispersion

  • hb_area(family = "gamma", engine = jax_engine()) uses vardir as the INLA engine does: the shape of each area is y2/Vy^2/V. Before, vardir was ignored with a message and a common shape was estimated, so the two engines fitted different models (estimates up to 2.6 posterior SD apart on a test example; now within 0.15 SD).
  • hb_area(family = "nbinomial") uses vardir. The size of each area follows from V=μ+μ2/nV = \mu + \mu^2/n as n=μ̂2/(V−μ̂)n = \hat\mu^2/(V - \hat\mu), with μ̂\hat\mu the posterior mean of a first fit that estimates one size, so the model is fitted twice (both engines). The direct count for μ\mu was too noisy (no better than one estimated size). In simulations (benchmarks/validation/dispersion_vardir.R, nb_size_prior.R) the 95% intervals covered 90-95% with vardir, with median relative errors up to a third smaller than without it.
  • The negative binomial size gets a half-normal(10) prior in the INLA engine too (as in jax_engine()), instead of INLA’s pc.mgamma(7). With one count per area the size follows its prior: pc.mgamma estimated sizes of 110-180 for true sizes 3-100 (nearly Poisson) and its intervals covered 76-92% when the overdispersion was real, against 90-97% now (benchmarks/validation/nb_size_prior.R). For nearly Poisson counts the intervals are now wider (up to 99%). The two engines now agree within 0.25 posterior SD on the NB model (0.72 before, with the different size priors). The warning without vardir no longer suggests family = "poisson": on negative binomial counts a Poisson model covered 68-75%.
  • jax_engine() starts the regression coefficients at 0 instead of the median of 15 draws of their prior: with the N(0,1000)N(0, 1000) prior that median can lie far out on a log or logit scale, where chains of a model with a sharp likelihood (the gamma model above) got stuck (R-hat 1.6-3.4 in 3 of 4 seeds; now at most 1.013 in 6 of 6).

SAR area effect in hb_area()

  • hb_area(spatial = "sar"): the simultaneous autoregressive area effect u=(I−ρW)−1εu = (I - \rho W)^{-1}\varepsilon of eblup_sfh(), i.e. its Bayesian counterpart ("slm" also filters the covariates). ρ\rho is uniform on |ρ|≤0.999|\rho| \le 0.999 and W is row-standardised. INLA fits it as its "slm" model with a zero covariate matrix (in "classic" mode); jax_engine() samples a non-centred uu through the eigendecomposition of W (a linear solve when W has a complex spectrum). Not combinable with the "type3"/"type4"/"separable" interactions.
    • With known vardir, INLA is within 0.004 posterior SD of the exact posterior (grid over σ\sigma and ρ\rho), and with 150 domains within 0.06 SD of eblup_sfh() (SD / mse\sqrt{\mathrm{mse}} 0.98-1.02, also for unsampled domains). The JAX engine agrees with INLA within 0.05 SD.

Unsampled domains and missing periods in eblup_stfh()

  • eblup_stfh() no longer requires a complete panel. Cells whose response is NA – missing periods of a sampled domain, or domains that are never sampled – stay in the data and are predicted. The model is defined on the full domain x time grid (the SAR effect on all domains of W, the AR(1) effect on all periods); the variance components are estimated by REML from the sampled cells (the marginal likelihood with the missing cells integrated out), and every cell gets the best linear unbiased predictor given the sampled data (Saei and Chambers, 2005; Benedetti et al., 2024). A missing period borrows from the other periods of its domain and from the neighbours; a domain never sampled is predicted from its neighbours (spatial kriging).
  • Analytical MSE for those cells: g1+g2+g3g_1 + g_2 + g_3, with g3g_3 from the exact derivative of the predictor in the variance components. The further correction of the plug-in g1g_1 is not applied: it is numerically unstable when ρ1\rho_1 approaches ±1\pm 1 or a variance component is weakly identified, and in Monte Carlo g1+g2+g3g_1 + g_2 + g_3 has a relative bias within a few percent and close to 95% coverage for these cells. The parametric bootstrap now draws the random effects on the full grid, refits on the sampled cells and covers every cell. df_eblup gains a sampled column; print() reports the number of predicted cells. The auxiliary variables must be known in every cell, and W must include the unsampled domains.
  • Results on complete panels are unchanged (bit-for-bit). The predictions and every MSE term are tested against a dense implementation, and benchmarks/sim_stfh_unsampled.R checks the MSE estimators by Monte Carlo.
  • The examples now use the full mys_panel and mys_proxmat (domains 21 and 25 are unsampled).

Area means in eblup_twofold()

  • eblup_twofold() now also estimates the area means θi=∑jwijθij\theta_i = \sum_j w_{ij}\theta_{ij}, returned in df_area (eblup_area, mse_area, rse_area, n_subareas, n_sampled). The new argument weight gives the sub-area weights (normalised within each area, equal by default, as in hb_twofold()); compute_area = FALSE skips them.
    • The analytical MSE is the second-order estimator of the sub-areas applied to the linear target (g1+g2+2g3g_1 + g_2 + 2g_3, minus the ML bias term). It includes the covariance of the sub-area errors through the area effect and β̂\hat\beta, so it is not ∑jwij2mseij\sum_j w_{ij}^2 \mathrm{mse}_{ij}. Areas without a sampled sub-area get the synthetic estimator. mse_type = "bootstrap" computes the area MSE from the same replicates.
    • Tested against a dense implementation (finite-difference g3g_3, REML information) and, with a weight on one sub-area, against the sub-area MSE. benchmarks/validation/twofold_area_mse.R checks the MSE estimators by Monte Carlo.

MSE argument, convergence and input checks

  • All EBLUP functions choose the MSE with mse_type, which includes "none" (no MSE; mse and rse are NA): eblup_fh() ("analytical", "none"), eblup_sfh() ("analytical", "pbmse", "npbmse", "none"), eblup_stfh() and eblup_twofold() ("analytical", "bootstrap", "none") and eblup_bhf() ("bootstrap", "none"). The chosen value is returned in mse_type.
    • eblup_sfh(mse_method = ) and compute_mse = of eblup_stfh() and eblup_bhf() are deprecated and still work with a warning (compute_mse = FALSE is mse_type = "none").
    • The MSE is now computed by default: eblup_stfh() gives the analytical MSE and eblup_bhf() the bootstrap MSE (both gave none before). Use mse_type = "none" for the previous output.
  • Convergence is reported as a warning that can be caught. Before, eblup_fh(), eblup_sfh(), eblup_stfh() and eblup_twofold() only printed a message and eblup_bhf() said nothing. INLA fits of hb_area(), hb_unit() and hb_twofold() now read convergence from the INLA mode search (ok, mode$mode.status; it was always TRUE), and hb_area(engine = "jax") warns when the largest split R-hat is 1.05 or more.
  • Inputs are checked before fitting, with a clear message:
    • vardir must be finite and positive in every sampled area (a missing value gave an error from the compiled code);
    • linearly dependent covariates stop the fit and name the aliased column (the compiled code used an approximate solution of a singular system);
    • there must be more sampled areas than coefficients (all MSEs were NA), and at least two sampled areas in eblup_twofold() and eblup_bhf();
    • W of eblup_sfh() and eblup_stfh() must be non-negative; a zero row (a domain without neighbours) or rows that do not sum to 1 give a warning, since the SAR model with rho in (-1, 1) assumes a row-standardised W, as ‘sae’ requires;
    • the same checks now cover the HB models. A missing covariate is an error in hb_area(), hb_twofold() and in the Xpop means of hb_unit(): INLA treats it as 0, so the estimate of that area was wrong without any message. hb_twofold() replaced a missing, zero or negative vardir of a sampled subarea by 1, and hb_area() stopped with an INLA error on a missing one; both now stop with the message of the EBLUP functions. hb_area() also rejects linearly dependent covariates;
    • a missing population mean in eblup_bhf() names the domain (it gave an internal error on the number of rows);
    • duplicated domain values give a warning in eblup_fh(), eblup_sfh() and hb_area() without time (in hb_area() such rows share one area effect).
  • A fixed seed of eblup_sfh(), eblup_stfh(), eblup_bhf() and eblup_twofold() no longer changes the random number stream of the session; the bootstrap MSEs are unchanged.
  • eblup_twofold() uses B = 100 and seed = -1 (no seed) by default, as the other EBLUP functions (it used B = 200 and seed = NULL; NULL still means no seed).
  • Gaussian models of hb_area(), hb_unit() and hb_twofold(), and the Leroux and SLM effects of hb_area() for any family, are fitted in INLA’s "classic" mode (Rue, Martino and Chopin, 2009); the other models keep INLA’s default "compact" mode (van Niekerk et al., 2023), which leaves the linear predictors out of the latent field and is designed for data-rich models. Gaussian models of hb_area() with a "type1" to "type4" interaction and three hyperparameters (a Besag or iid area effect, a random walk or iid in time) also integrate over a grid of hyperparameters. Larger models (temporal = "ar1", or a BYM, BYM2, Leroux or SLM area effect) keep INLA’s default integration: the grid grows exponentially with the number of hyperparameters (with AR(1), 30 s and 13 min for 12 areas against about 1 s) and was validated only for three. The choices rest on comparisons with the exact posterior (numerical integration over the variances) and with long Stan runs with the same model and priors (scripts in benchmarks/validation):
    • Gaussian: the compact mode overstated the posterior SDs by up to 18% (hb_area(), when the area variance is small relative to vardir; it was accurate on mys), 8-15% (hb_unit(), cornsoybean) and 10% (hb_twofold()), and hb_unit() gave different county means on identical calls (up to 3 hectares and 13% in the SDs). In the classic mode the posterior means were within 0.07 posterior SD and the SDs within 0.91-1.03 times the reference, at the same speed. With a space-time interaction both modes overstated the SDs by 6-13%; classic with the grid matched Stan (means within 0.04 SD, SDs within 2%) and takes 5-8 times longer.
    • Binomial, Poisson, beta and gamma: both modes matched Stan (compact: means within 0.16 posterior SD, SDs within 0.95-1.08 times), and the classic mode was much slower for many areas or units (beta with 2000 areas: 32 s against 1.3 s; hb_unit() binomial with 4000 units: 72 s against 2.6 s). The exception is the Leroux and SLM effects, where compact moved Poisson means by 0.12-0.15 SD (classic: within 0.03 SD).
    • With a small area variance, the classic summary of that variance (random_effect_var) is biased downwards while the area estimates are accurate; this is documented. inla_engine(inla.mode = , control.inla = ) overrides the settings.
  • hb_area() space-time interactions with a random walk in time are identified as in Knorr-Held (2000). INLA’s default constraints left one level (rw1) or one linear trend (rw2) per domain with a flat prior: a domain without direct estimates had a posterior SD of 36-58 (other domains about 0.4) in the type IV interaction (rw1, rw2) and the type II interaction (rw2). These interactions are now a generic0 term with the scaled Kronecker structure and all the constraints (sums over domains per period and over periods per domain, and linear trends per domain for rw2); they match Stan with the same constraints. The "separable" field with a random walk in time, which has no spatial main effect to carry the domain levels, and the "domain-specific" rw2, which has no common trend, now stop with an error suggesting temporal = "ar1", "type4" or "type2".
  • hb_area(family = "nbinomial") warns that with one count per area the overdispersion and the area effect are only weakly identified: INLA’s posterior means were off by up to 0.6 posterior SD against Stan in every mode. "poisson" or engine = "jax" (MCMC) is suggested.
  • CAR models (spatial = "besag", "bym", "bym2", "leroux") of hb_area(), hb_unit() and hb_twofold() use only the pattern W > 0. A dense W such as distance-decay weights becomes a (nearly) complete graph and an almost unstructured spatial effect; it now gives a warning. mys_proxmat is such a matrix (all 861 pairs linked): its documentation said it was based on contiguous boundaries, and the examples and vignettes now fit CAR models on a 4-nearest- neighbour graph of the sim_area centroids. mys_proxmat remains suited to the SAR models.
  • hb_unit(family = "binomial" / "poisson") warns that the domain means are approximate. The non-sampled part is predicted at the mean covariates, inv_link(xbar' beta + u_d), which is biased for the mean of inv_link(x' beta + u_d) over the units: in a simulation -8% (binomial) and -16% (Poisson) for the sampled domains, with 90% and 78% coverage of the 95% intervals. Unbiased estimation needs unit-level population covariates (Molina and Rao, 2010); see ?hb_unit. The Gaussian model is not affected.
  • hb_twofold(weight = ) warns about missing or negative weights (they get weight 0 in df_area, as before, but silently).
  • compare_sae() between a Hierarchical Bayes and an EBLUP model no longer calls the model with the smaller posterior variance “more efficient”: it reports which one has the lower reported uncertainty and notes that a posterior variance and an MSE are not the same quantity.
  • Posterior draws of the INLA engine are reproducible: inla_engine(seed = 1L) is the new default (it was 0L, INLA’s random seed), and the seed is also set on the R side, since INLA draws the hyperparameter configurations with R’s RNG; the session’s random number stream is restored. This affects the area aggregates of hb_twofold() (their SD changed by up to 9% between identical calls), posterior self-benchmarking in hb_area() and benchmark_sae().
  • New vignette “Sub-Area Level Estimation with Two-Fold Models” (eblup_twofold(), hb_twofold()); the unit-level vignette covers hb_unit().

Fixes before the 1.0.0 release

  • eblup_fh() and eblup_sfh() say with a message when the random effect variance is estimated as 0 (the (RE)ML estimate is truncated at 0, as in ‘sae’): the EBLUPs are then the synthetic estimates and the MSE estimates can understate their error (Li and Lahiri, 2010).
  • sim_area_data(), sim_series_data() and sim_spatial_weights() restore the random number stream of the session after using seed; they replaced it before. The simulated data are unchanged.
  • benchmark_sae() documentation: the references are corrected. Two-stage benchmarking cites Ghosh and Steorts (2013), optimal benchmarking Datta et al. (2011) and Bell, Datta and Ghosh (2013); the citations of You and Rao (2002), Berg and Fuller (2014) and a non-existent “Steorts, Hall and Ghosh (2014)” are removed.
  • Examples: eblup_bhf() no longer needs ‘dplyr’, the eblup_stfh() example of sim_series_data() runs, eblup_sfh() uses mse_type instead of the deprecated mse_method, and the S3 methods (print(), summary(), coef(), fitted(), residuals(), plot(), autoplot() of diagnose()) have examples.
  • The website moved to https://ridsonap.is-a.dev/fastsae/.
  • benchmark_sae() stops when a target or national_target is missing or not finite, or a weight is missing. Before, a target of NA (for example a weighted.mean() of direct estimates that include unsampled domains) silently made every benchmarked estimate NA.
  • A subset of a benchmark_sae() result, such as bm[, c("domain", "benchmarked")], prints as a data frame. It printed the header of the full result with the method “Ratio” whatever method had been used, because [ drops the attributes that the header reads.
  • hb_area(st_interaction = "type2" / "type3" / "type4") now fit with INLA. They always failed before (the interaction reused the index of a main effect, which INLA rejects), and with spatial = "none" the type III/IV interaction was silently dropped. The interaction is now a separate term on copied indices: one temporal process per domain (type II), or an ICAR field per period (type III) or evolving with temporal (type IV). Types III and IV need a structured spatial effect and stop with a clear message otherwise.
  • hb_area(spatial = "leroux", st_interaction = "separable") fits instead of crashing inside INLA: the grouped Leroux field uses INLA’s besagproper2, the same model as generic1.
  • inla_engine(link = ) is used. It was accepted but ignored; it now sets the link of the likelihood ("probit", "cloglog" and "loglog" for binomial and beta), checked against the family. The posterior draws for self-benchmarking and benchmark_sae() use the matching inverse link, and the link is returned in link.
  • hb_area(spatial = "bym"): random_effect_var is the variance of the spatial component (it was the iid one). Interaction terms no longer feed random_effect_var, rho or rho_time, and with st_interaction = "separable" the AR(1) group correlation is returned in rho_time.
  • hb_area() objects have class c("fastsae_hb_area", "fastsae_hb", "fastsae"), like hb_unit() and hb_twofold().
  • The documentation of inla_engine(prior_prec = ) explains the different defaults: the PC prior pc.prec(1, 0.01) of hb_area() and hb_twofold() assumes an area standard deviation of order 1 (proportions, rates, log scales), while hb_unit() keeps the vague loggamma(0.01, 0.01) because unit-level responses are often on a raw scale.
  • goodness of eblup_fh(), eblup_sfh(), eblup_stfh() and eblup_twofold() follows one convention. loglikelihood is the full Gaussian log-likelihood at the estimates, and AIC/BIC are computed from it for ML and REML fits, as in ‘sae’ and Marhuenda, Morales and Pardo (2014): the restricted likelihood depends on the covariates, so it cannot compare models with different covariates and is not reported. goodness always has these three elements.
    • eblup_twofold(): loglikelihood, AIC and BIC of REML fits were based on the restricted log-likelihood and now use the full one; BIC uses the number of sampled subareas (it used the number of areas).
    • eblup_stfh(): the element loglike is renamed loglikelihood, as in the other models.
  • eblup_twofold(): a negative second-order MSE estimate (possible with the ML bias correction) is set to NA with a warning instead of giving a NaN RSE.
  • eblup_stfh() reports convergence = FALSE when the fit ends at invalid variance components (it reported TRUE with no estimates). The documentation explains why the model is fitted by REML only (as in Marhuenda, Molina and Morales 2013 and sae::eblupSTFH()) and that tvalue is a z-statistic.

Statistical corrections (mathematical audit)

  • eblup_stfh(): the analytical g3g_3 was computed with the wrong matrix orientation ((KaΨVΨKb)ii(K_a \Psi V \Psi K_b)_{ii} instead of ψi2(KaVKb)ii\psi_i^2 (K_a V K_b)_{ii}), which is wrong whenever vardir is heterogeneous. g3g_3 now uses the exact derivative of the EBLUP, ∂θ̃/∂θa=ΨPVaPy\partial\tilde\theta/\partial\theta_a = \Psi P V_a P y, and the REML information at the final estimates.

  • eblup_stfh() bootstrap MSE: the variance components are now re-estimated in every replicate (before, they were held fixed, so the bootstrap missed the g3g_3 contribution), and the SAR effects are generated with the lower Cholesky factor (before, Var(u1)=RR′≠Ω1\mathrm{Var}(u_1) = RR' \ne \Omega_1).

  • eblup_stfh() now sorts the panel internally into the domain-major order the model requires and returns results in the caller’s row order. Before, unsorted input was silently mis-specified – including the time-major mys_panel used in the examples, tests and vignette (where sae::eblupSTFH(), which assumes domain-major data, gave the same wrong fit).

  • eblup_stfh(): when the classical Fisher scoring fails, or converges to a negative variance that would only be truncated to 0, the fit switches to constrained REML (variances >= 0, |rho| <= 0.999; projected scoring with step halving), which returns the actual constrained maximiser. Convergence in a simulation went from 63% to 99% of the replicates; fits on which the classical iteration converges to an interior point are unchanged (identical to sae::eblupSTFH()). A correlation whose variance is 0 is unidentified and gets an NA standard error.

  • eblup_stfh() bootstrap: non-converged replicates are replaced by new draws until B valid replicates are obtained (as in the SFH bootstrap).

  • eblup_twofold(): the analytical MSE estimator is now g1+g2+2g3g_1 + g_2 + 2 g_3 (REML) and g1+g2+2g3−bML′∇g1g_1 + g_2 + 2 g_3 - b_{ML}'\nabla g_1 (ML); before it was g1+g2+g3g_1 + g_2 + g_3, which ignores the downward bias of the plug-in g1g_1. The REML Fisher information now includes the cross-area terms.

  • eblup_sfh() with unsampled domains: the SAR process is defined on all domains of W, so the sampled domains are now fitted with the marginal covariance σ2Σfull[s,s]\sigma^2 \Sigma_{full}[s,s] (before: the SAR built from the sub-matrix W[s,s]), consistent with the kriging of the unsampled domains and the bootstrap.

  • eblup_sfh(): an upper-boundary ρ̂=0.999\hat\rho = 0.999 is no longer mapped to 11 (singular for a row-standardised W); bootstrap replicates are no longer rejected when estimates exceed 1e6 (scale-dependent check); npbmse no longer fails when σ̂u2=0\hat\sigma^2_u = 0.

  • hb_unit() with popsize_var: the non-sampled part is now predicted at the non-sampled covariate mean x‾d,r=(NdX‾d−ndx‾d,s)/(Nd−nd)\bar x_{d,r} = (N_d \bar X_d - n_d \bar x_{d,s})/(N_d - n_d) (before: at X‾d\bar X_d), and its posterior SD includes σe2/(Nd−nd)\sigma_e^2/(N_d - n_d).

  • hb_unit() (Gaussian, non-spatial): INLA’s posterior mode search now starts at the REML estimates of the nested error model. Under the vague log-gamma prior it could stall near σu2=0\sigma^2_u = 0 depending on the number of threads (e.g. σ̂u2≈1\hat\sigma^2_u \approx 1 instead of ≈68\approx 68 on cornsoybean). A control.mode passed through inla_engine() takes precedence.

  • benchmark_sae(method = "optimal"): the adjustment is now proportional to wiMSEiw_i\,\mathrm{MSE}_i, the minimiser of ∑i(θi′−θ̂i)2/MSEi\sum_i (\theta_i' - \hat\theta_i)^2/\mathrm{MSE}_i subject to the benchmark (before: MSEi/wi\mathrm{MSE}_i / w_i). Results are unchanged for equal weights.

  • eblup_twofold() with one subarea per area (only s2v + s2u identified): Fisher scoring uses the pseudo-inverse of the singular information.

  • eblup_bhf(): the bootstrap MSE now uses the same population means (popnmean_xpop) as the estimate.

  • eblup_fh(transform = "log"): documentation now describes the back-transformation accurately (conditional-mean correction exp⁡(μ̃+g1/2)\exp(\tilde\mu + g_1/2) with delta-method MSE; not the full Slud-Maiti second-order correction), and self-benchmarking warns that the constraint holds on the log scale only.

  • eblup_fh(transform = "log"): unsampled domains now always use the synthetic correction exp⁡(x′β̂+σ̂u2/2)\exp(x'\hat\beta + \hat\sigma^2_u/2), even when their vardir is supplied.

  • HB models: reported variance components are posterior means of the variance, E[1/τ∣y]E[1/\tau \mid y], instead of 1/E[τ∣y]1/E[\tau \mid y].

  • eblup_stfh() analytical MSE now includes the second-derivative term g4g_4 (V is nonlinear in ρ1,ρ2\rho_1, \rho_2), as the SFH MSE does: mse = g1 + g2 + 2 g3 - g4, with g4 returned. Simulation: relative bias -1.7% (was +2.4% without g4g_4, -6.1% without g3g_3).

  • eblup_sfh(): when the classical Fisher scoring fails or ends with σ̂2<0\hat\sigma^2 < 0, the (RE)ML likelihood is maximised under the constraints (as for eblup_stfh()), also inside the bootstrap. An estimate at ρ=−0.999\rho = -0.999 is reported as −1-1 only when I+WI + W is non-singular (not for bipartite graphs such as a rook grid, where it made the bootstrap MSE explode).

  • eblup_sfh() unsampled (kriged) domains: the analytical MSE now includes g3g_3 (exact derivative of the kriging predictor) and the second-order bias of the plug-in g1g_1 (and the ML bias term): g1 + g2 + g3 - tr(I^{-1} Hess g1)/2. Simulation (REML): relative bias -3.8% (was -7.5%).

  • eblup_sfh() / eblup_stfh() analytical MSE: a correlation estimated on the boundary (|ρ̂|≥0.999|\hat\rho| \ge 0.999, or reported as −1-1) is treated as fixed – only the information block of the other parameters is inverted – because the Prasad-Rao expansion is not valid there and could explode. The SE of such a ρ\rho is NA. For SFH this departs from sae::mseSFH in that case only (interior estimates still agree exactly).

  • eblup_sfh(method = "ML") analytical MSE: g3g_3 and the ML bias term bML=12I−1hb_{ML} = \frac12 I^{-1} h now use the ML information instead of the REML one (as sae::mseSFH does). With σ̂2≈0\hat\sigma^2 \approx 0 and ρ̂≈1\hat\rho \approx 1 the REML choice made the bias term explode (MSE up to 10610^6 in simulations); with few domains the ML information also reduced the median MSE bias (e.g. +3.6% vs +6.5%, m=36m = 36). The ML MSE therefore no longer equals sae::mseSFH; REML is unchanged.

  • eblup_stfh() is much faster: REML scores and Fisher information are computed from the block structure of VV (domain blocks plus a rank-DD spatial part) without forming M×MM \times M matrices (O(TD3+M(D+p)2)O(T D^3 + M(D+p)^2) instead of O(M3)O(M^3) per iteration; identical results). Fitting the 40×1140 \times 11mys_panel went from about 7.7 s to 0.4 s, and the parametric bootstrap (which re-estimates the model in every replicate) from about 2.4 s to 0.4 s per replicate.

  • hb_area(self_benchmark = TRUE) now benchmarks every posterior draw by default (benchmark_method = "posterior"; difference / logit / ratio adjustment by family), so the constraint is exact for every likelihood and SD / credible intervals refer to the benchmarked estimator. Benchmark targets are computed on the parameter scale (proportions for binomial, rates for counts with exposure); before, the WFQ targets used counts while the estimates were proportions / rates. benchmark_method = "wfq" keeps the previous augmented-model approach.

  • eblup_fh(transform = "log", self_benchmark = TRUE): ratio benchmarking of the back-transformed estimates on the original scale (exact), instead of a WFQ constraint that only held on the log scale.

  • benchmark_sae(): the group MSE used by the hierarchical “optimal” method now includes the covariances between area prediction errors (full MSE matrix for FH, SFH, STFH and INLA area-level HB fits), and the output has a new mse_benchmarked column, the first-order MSE of the benchmarked estimates (msei−2ki(Mw)i+adji2mse_i - 2 k_i (Mw)_i + adj_i^2; within about 1% of the empirical MSE in a simulation).

  • diagnose(): the Brown et al. (2001) goodness-of-fit statistic WW now uses an upper-tail χ2\chi^2 decision (as emdi::compare.fh); the former two-sided interval flagged every correct FH fit in a simulation, because WW is conservative. The bias regression of the direct on the model estimates is now descriptive (brown_test$bias_regression: alpha, beta, standard errors, R2R^2) instead of an F test of α=0,β=1\alpha = 0, \beta = 1, which rejected 93% of correct FH fits (the slope exceeds 1 for shrinkage estimators); it no longer affects status. simulation_metrics$rrmse is the relative RMSE across domains (mean_rrmse duplicated mean_abs_rb). DIC/WAIC/marginal likelihood are now also read for hb_unit() and hb_twofold() fits, and CPO/PIT are only used when they are per domain.

  • spatial_test(): the FH vs spatial FH comparison uses ML fits, so the likelihood ratio and AIC/BIC are computed from ML log-likelihoods at ML estimates (before: at REML estimates). The recommendation now rests on a single test at level alpha (decision_test: the likelihood ratio test when vardir is given, otherwise the LM-error test); requiring any of three tests recommended a spatial model for 9% of non-spatial data sets at alpha = 0.05. The Moran’s I, LM-error and LM-lag statistics are unchanged and agree with spdep.

  • diagnose(): standardised residuals are (y−θ̂)/vardir−MSE(y - \hat\theta)/\sqrt{vardir - MSE} (the variance of y−θ̂y - \hat\theta) instead of /vardir/\sqrt{vardir}, which shrank them (sd 0.76 under a correct FH model) and hid outliers in the residual and Q-Q plots.

  • Reliability tiers (add_reliability_flags(), export_sae(), map_sae(), compare_sae(), autoplot(type = "rse")) default to the BPS-Statistics Indonesia criteria: RSE <= 25% reliable, 25% < RSE <= 50% use with caution, RSE > 50% unreliable (was 20%/30%, documented as the BPS standard). map_sae(type = "reliability") now uses its thresholds argument (they were ignored).

  • benchmark_sae(type = "total") in a hierarchical benchmark without group targets: the group aggregates are weighted totals (they were weighted means, on the wrong scale for stage 1).

Breaking changes and clean-up

  • mys_proxmat is now the row-standardised 4-nearest-neighbour graph of the 42 areas (symmetric, 4 to 8 neighbours per area, built from the sim_area centroids by data-raw/mys_proxmat.R). It was a dense distance-decay matrix with almost equal weights (largest weight per row 0.03-0.04, against 1/41 = 0.024 for equal weights), which the CAR models of hb_area() read as a complete graph. Results that use mys_proxmat change. On mys the SAR correlation of eblup_sfh() stays at its bound -1 with either matrix: the residuals of mys have no positive spatial autocorrelation. sim_area and sim_panel are unchanged (simulated with the old matrix).
  • benchmark(), a plain alias of benchmark_sae(), is removed; use benchmark_sae().
  • The leftover handling of df_ebp/ebp result tables (from the removed ebp_area()) is removed from the methods and utilities; results are in df_hb (HB) or df_eblup (EBLUP).
  • diagnose() returns brown_test$bias_regression instead of brown_test$wald_test and simulation_metrics$rrmse instead of mean_rrmse (see above).

Other fixes in the utilities

  • map_sae() works with any name of the sf geometry column (it assumed "geometry"), labels HB fits correctly (they were labelled “EBP-”), and stops with a clear message for panel or sub-area tables with repeated domains instead of mis-merging them.
  • compare_sae() and autoplot() plots label panel and sub-area rows uniquely (repeated domains made some plots fail or overlap); autoplot() of an unnamed list of models names them.
  • print()/summary() show the estimation method of eblup_fh() and eblup_twofold() (REML or ML; was “eblup”) and describe eblup_stfh(model = "S") correctly.
  • export_sae() lists both variance components of two-fold models in the model summary.

Performance

  • hb_twofold() (INLA): the area aggregates in df_area took most of the fit time. INLA::inla.posterior.sample() with a seed runs the inla program once per hyperparameter configuration (~0.3 s each): 143 configurations for the Gaussian model (45 s with 15 areas) and 36-39 for the binomial and Poisson models (22-34 s), for only 200 draws.
    • Gaussian: the aggregates are INLA linear combinations of the sub-area predictors, with exact posterior marginals (45 s -> 6 s); the area SDs agree with 4000 draws within their Monte Carlo error.
    • Binomial and Poisson: the draws are taken in R from the Gaussian approximation of the latent field at each of INLA’s configurations, chosen by their posterior weight as INLA does, and inla_engine(draws = ) now defaults to 2000 instead of 200: under a second for the draws, and reproducible with seed. With 200 draws the aggregate interval bounds were off by up to 0.4-0.6 posterior SD against 10000 INLA draws, with 2000 by at most 0.17. INLA’s skewness correction is not applied; with 20000 draws it moved the aggregates less than the Monte Carlo error. INLA’s own sampler is still used if the fit has no stored configurations.
  • benchmark_sae(): the MSE covariance between areas is applied as a matrix-free operator (FH: O(np2)O(n p^2), no n×nn \times n matrices). FH with m=2000m = 2000: 9.4 s / 490 MB -> 0.002 s / 1.7 MB; m=20000m = 20000 now runs in about 0.01 s.
  • eblup_bhf(): the REML/ML fit and the bootstrap MSE now run in C++ (src/eblup_bhf_core.cpp). The likelihood is profiled to γ=σu2/σe2≥0\gamma = \sigma_u^2/\sigma_e^2 \ge 0 and evaluated from within-domain cross-products and domain means (O(Dp2)O(Dp^2) per evaluation, independent of the number of units); the maximum is found from a log-grid scan plus Brent refinement, so σu2=0\sigma_u^2 = 0 is handled exactly. Estimates agree with lme4/sae up to their optimiser tolerance (deviance never worse), and the bootstrap uses the same random draws as before, so MSEs agree with the previous lme4-based implementation to about 1e-5 for a given seed. Bootstrap: cornsoybean B=200B = 200 0.64 s -> 0.005 s; D=300D = 300, n=6000n = 6000, B=100B = 100 0.96 s -> 0.035 s. n_threads now runs replicates in parallel (results do not depend on it); for small models R’s sequential RNG dominates the run time.
  • eblup_bhf() output: fit$lme (the lmerMod object) is replaced by fit$residuals (unit-level conditional residuals, used by residuals()); estcoef standard errors are (X′V̂−1X)−1(X'\hat V^{-1}X)^{-1} as in lme4. Rank-deficient designs now give an explicit error.
  • eblup_sfh() (fit, analytical MSE, kriging and the bootstrap refits) no longer forms any D×DD \times D inverse or D3D^3 product. With A=(I−ρW′)(I−ρW)A = (I - \rho W')(I - \rho W) and M=A+σ2E′Ψ−1EM = A + \sigma^2 E'\Psi^{-1}E (both sparse), V−1V^{-1}, GV−1GV^{-1}, g1=σ2diag(M−1)g_1 = \sigma^2 \mathrm{diag}(M^{-1}), the scores/information, g3g_3, g4g_4, the ML bias and the kriging terms follow from Cholesky solves with AA and MM (src/sar_engine.h; Eigen sparse LDL′LDL' with AMD ordering, dense factorisations when WW itself is dense, e.g. distance weights). Results are unchanged (relative differences below 2e-10). Analytical: D=400D = 400 2.2 s -> 0.10 s, D=1600D = 1600 80 s -> 2.5 s, D=2500D = 2500 about 6 s; bootstrap (D=400D = 400, B=20B = 20): 16 s -> 1.3 s. RcppEigen is added to LinkingTo.
  • eblup_stfh(): the final step (Fisher information at the estimates, SEs, g1g_1-g4g_4 of the analytical MSE) no longer forms M×MM \times M matrices (M=DTM = DT); it uses the same structured representation of VV as the iterations (A−1A^{-1} block diagonal, P=A−1−UWU′P = A^{-1} - U W U' with U=[A−1Z,V−1X]U = [A^{-1}Z, V^{-1}X] whose A−1ZA^{-1}Z part has one non-zero per row). The scoring step also exploits the diagonal blocks of U′ZU'Z and U′EUU'EU and the sparsity of C=2ρW′W−W−W′C = 2\rho W'W - W - W'. Results are unchanged (relative differences below 3e-11). T=5T = 5: D=250D = 250 28 s -> 1.6 s, D=500D = 500 about 4 min -> 10 s, D=1000D = 1000 75 s.
  • create_weights(): distances for knn, distance and idw are computed in blocks of rows (at most about 1M distances at a time) instead of a full D×DD \times D distance matrix, and the weight matrix is filled once from the neighbour pairs (no intermediate 0/1 matrix and no normalisation copies; idw styles are applied per block). The result is the same matrix as before (identical, or within 1e-16 for idw). Peak memory at D=10000D = 10000: queen 2.3 GB -> 0.8 GB, knn 3.1 GB -> 0.8 GB, distance 3.8 GB -> 0.8 GB, i.e. essentially the returned matrix itself (764 MB).

Bug fixes

  • create_weights() with a coordinate matrix whose columns are named X/Y (e.g. from sf::st_coordinates()) failed with “undefined columns selected”; coordinate column names are now matched case-insensitively.

Major New Features & Enhancements

  • Two-Fold Subarea EBLUP (eblup_twofold):
    • Implements nested two-fold sub-area level models (Torabi & Rao, 2014) with area effects viv_i and sub-area effects uiju_{ij}.
    • Ultra-fast Fisher-scoring algorithms in C++ for REML and ML estimation.
    • Analytical Prasad-Rao MSE (g1+g2+2g3g_1 + g_2 + 2 g_3 for REML, plus the bias correction for ML) with exact matrix derivation and multi-threaded parametric bootstrap MSE.
    • Automatic prediction for non-sampled subareas using area-level random effects and regression synthetic estimation.
  • Hierarchical Bayes Two-Fold Subarea Models (hb_twofold):
    • Bayesian nested two-fold sub-area models via INLA.
    • Supports Gaussian, Binomial (logit link), and Poisson (log rate) likelihoods.
    • Area-level random effects support IID or spatial structures (BYM2, Besag).
    • Simultaneous posterior estimation for subareas (df_hb) and weighted area aggregates (df_area) with full Monte Carlo uncertainty propagation.
  • Hierarchical Bayes Area-Level Models (hb_area):
    • Fast Bayesian inference powered by Integrated Nested Laplace Approximations (INLA).
    • Supports 6 probability distributions for non-Gaussian area indicators: Gaussian, Binomial (logit link with trials), Poisson (log rate with exposure/offsets), Negative Binomial, Beta, and Gamma.
    • Spatial random effects: BYM2 (Besag-York-Mollié 2 with PC-priors) and Besag/CAR models.
    • Automatic handling of unsampled domains and domain-specific variance predictions.
  • Hierarchical Bayes Unit-Level Models (hb_unit):
    • Bayesian unit-level Battese-Harter-Fuller (BHF) and generalized linear mixed models via INLA.
    • Supports Gaussian, Binomial (binary unit outcomes), and Poisson (count outcomes).
    • Domain random effects with optional spatial structures (BYM2, Besag).
    • Finite population adjustments when domain population sizes (NdN_d) are supplied.
    • Seamless handling of both domain-level population means and micro-level census data.
  • Two-Stage Hierarchical Benchmarking (benchmark_sae):
    • Unified calibration framework for multi-level administrative structures (e.g., Domain -> Province -> National).
    • Implements Ratio, Difference, Optimal Variance-Weighted Quadratic Loss (Datta et al. 2011; Steorts et al. 2014), and Constrained Logit benchmarking (Berg & Fuller 2014).
  • Comprehensive Diagnostics & Visualization:
    • diagnose(): Brown et al. (2001) goodness-of-fit and bias diagnostics, residual analysis, spatial autocorrelation tests (Moran’s I), and official statistical reliability classification (BPS standards).
    • compare_sae(): Tabular model comparison across information criteria and error metrics.
    • map_sae(): Spatial thematic choropleth maps integrated with sf.
    • export_sae(): Export estimation results with full statistical metadata to Excel (openxlsx/writexl) and CSV.
  • Simulation Utilities:
    • sim_area_data() and sim_series_data(), which return the simulated spatial weights (W, W_std; spatial_type and the number of neighbours k choose the graph).
  • Reliability & Performance:
    • High-performance C++ core (RcppArmadillo and OpenMP) with strict validation checks.

fastsae 0.1.0
